title: How we keep a 230-page static site fast and internally linked with one Python build script
author: DiziGoo Digital
summary: Our agency site has about 230 pages: services, software, guides and city pages. Instead of a CMS, one Python script builds every page as plain HTML. Here is what worked for speed and for search. 1. Compress images at build time The build converts every JPG and PNG to WebP (quality around 74, lower for blog photos) and rewrites the HTML to point at the WebP files. Pages stay light without any manual work. 2. Generate internal links from the page list Orphan pages are easy to create when you add pages by hand. After all pages are built, the script groups them (services, software, guides, cities) and appends a small related-links block to each page: the next few siblings in the same group, a few pages from other groups, and the key hubs. A quick check afterwards counts inbound links per page, and every page now has at least five. 3. Keep the sitemap honest The XML sitemap and the human sitemap page come from the same page list, so the counts match. Queued posts that are not published yet stay out of both until they go live. 4. Verify after every deploy We fetch a handful of live URLs with curl and grep for the new markup, then submit changed URLs through IndexNow and Search Console. It takes a minute and catches stale caches. If you are curious how the result looks, our local pages for Pilibhit and Bareilly are here: https://dizigoo.com/locations/india/pilibhit/ and https://dizigoo.com/locations/india/bareilly/ . We are DiziGoo, a digital marketing and software team from Uttar Pradesh: https://dizigoo.com/

title: Getting the right favicon for 1,000 domains is harder than it looks
author: COFFEE CAT
summary: If you have a list of company domains (a CRM export, a directory, a bookmarks app) and want a small logo next to each one, the obvious approach is https://example.com/favicon.ico . It works for maybe half of the sites, and the result is often a blurry 16 px image. Here is what I learned while building a bulk favicon extractor, and the rules I ended up with. 1. /favicon.ico is the fallback, not the answer Most modern sites declare several icons in the HTML head: <link rel = "icon" href = "/favicon-32x32.png" sizes = "32x32" > <link rel = "apple-touch-icon" href = "/apple-touch-icon.png" sizes = "180x180" > <link rel = "mask-icon" href = "/safari-pinned-tab.svg" color = "#000" > <link rel = "manifest" href = "/site.webmanifest" > The 180 px apple-touch-icon is usually the best-looking one. Some sites have no /favicon.ico at all and only declare icons in <link> tags. 2. The biggest icons live in the web-app manifest The 192 px and 512 px icons are often only listed in site.webmanifest : { "icons" : [ { "src" : "/android-chrome-512x512.png" , "sizes" : "512x512" } ] } If you skip the manifest, you miss the highest-resolution logo the site has. 3. Never trust the sizes attribute Declared sizes are frequently wrong: sizes="192x192" on a 32 px file, or icons that return 404. The only reliable way is to download each candidate and read the real dimensions: from io import BytesIO from PIL import Image def measure ( data : bytes ) : with Image . open ( BytesIO ( data ) ) as im : if im . format == "ICO" : # .ico files hold several frames return max ( im . info [ "sizes" ] , key = lambda s : s [ 0 ] * s [ 1 ] ) return im . size 4. ICO files contain several images A favicon.ico typically holds 16, 32 and 48 px frames, and other tools may give you the first (smallest) one. Pillow (checked with 12.0) opens the largest frame by default and lists all of them in im.info["sizes"] . To pick a frame explicitly, assign it to im.size before loading: im = Image . open ( BytesIO ( data ) ) # an .ico file im . size = max ( im . info [ "sizes" ] , key = lambda s : s [ 0 ] * s [ 1 ] ) im . load ( ) im . convert ( "RGBA" ) . save ( "icon.png" ) 5. Ranking rule that worked Prefer icons that were actually downloaded and measured (raster). Then the largest measured edge. Ties: apple-touch-icon / manifest over icon over the default /favicon.ico ; SVG mask icons last (they are single-color silhouettes). 6. Be polite at scale Respect robots.txt . Cap downloads per site (8 icon candidates was enough). Put a hard deadline per site: some servers trickle bytes forever. Refuse private and loopback addresses if users can submit URLs. Don't want to build it? I packaged all of the above as an Apify Actor: paste domains, get every declared icon with measured sizes and the best one saved as PNG. You pay per website where an icon was found, with no start fee: https://apify.com/chivalrous_skyline_vtd/favicon-extractor The rules above are the useful part, though. They work in any language.

title: How to Check Every Page on Your Site for Duplicate H1 Tags with Python
author: Evgenii Kaya
summary: When we audited all 199 content URLs on our site, we did not start with Search Console. We started with the HTML the server actually sends, and with a short checklist for each page. One of the simplest checks on that list is also one of the easiest to skip: how many H1 headings does this page have? You want one. A template can add a second without anyone typing it, and once that happens it tends to happen on every page that uses the same template. Here is the small script we used to find that, and to see whether the extras shared a class, which usually means one template fix rather than a page-by-page cleanup. What the script does It reads every URL from your XML sitemap, including sitemap index files, and downloads the raw HTML of each page. It removes scripts, styles, templates and HTML comments, so an <h1> inside a code string or a commented-out block doesn't count. Then it counts the H1s and records their text, their CSS classes and their parent's classes, and writes everything to a CSV. The class columns are the useful part. If the pages with more than one H1 all share the same pair of classes, you have found a template to fix, not a pile of one-off pages. The code You'll need requests , beautifulsoup4 and lxml : pip install requests beautifulsoup4 lxml import csv import sys import time from xml . etree import ElementTree import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup , Comment HEADERS = { "User-Agent" : "Mozilla/5.0 (h1-audit)" } NS = { "sm" : "http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9" } def get_urls ( sitemap_url ) : root = ElementTree . fromstring ( requests . get ( sitemap_url , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20 ) . content ) children = root . findall ( "sm:sitemap/sm:loc" , NS ) if children : return [ url for loc in children for url in get_urls ( loc . text . strip ( ) ) ] return [ loc . text . strip ( ) for loc in root . findall ( "sm:url/sm:loc" , NS ) ] def get_h1s ( url ) : response = requests . get ( url , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20 , allow_redirects = False ) soup = BeautifulSoup ( response . text , "lxml" ) for tag in soup ( [ "script" , "style" , "noscript" , "template" ] ) : tag . decompose ( ) for comment in soup . find_all ( string = lambda text : isinstance ( text , Comment ) ) : comment . extract ( ) h1s = [ ] for h1 in soup . find_all ( "h1" ) : text = " " . join ( h1 . get_text ( " " ) . split ( ) ) classes = "." . join ( h1 . get ( "class" , [ ] ) ) parent = h1 . parent . get ( "class" , [ ] ) if h1 . parent else [ ] h1s . append ( ( text , classes , "." . join ( parent ) ) ) return response . status_code , h1s def main ( ) : urls = get_urls ( sys . argv [ 1 ] ) limit = int ( sys . argv [ 2 ] ) if len ( sys . argv ) > 2 else None urls = urls [ : limit ] problems = 0 with open ( "h1_audit.csv" , "w" , newline = "" , encoding = "utf-8" ) as file : writer = csv . writer ( file ) writer . writerow ( [ "url" , "status" , "h1_count" , "h1_texts" , "h1_classes" , "parent_classes" ] ) for url in urls : status , h1s = get_h1s ( url ) if len ( h1s ) != 1 : problems += 1 writer . writerow ( [ url , status , len ( h1s ) , " | " . join ( text for text , _ , _ in h1s ) , " | " . join ( cls for _ , cls , _ in h1s ) , " | " . join ( parent for _ , _ , parent in h1s ) , ] ) time . sleep ( 0.5 ) print ( f "Checked {len(urls)} pages, {problems} without exactly one H1. See h1_audit.csv" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) Run it with your sitemap and, optionally, a page limit for a quick test: python h1_audit.py https://example.com/sitemap.xml 20 A few details that matter The script reads the HTML the server sends, which is what most crawlers see first. If your site renders content in the browser with JavaScript, you'll need a headless browser instead. Don't follow redirects. With allow_redirects=False , a URL that has already moved shows up with its real status instead of quietly reporting the H1 of a different page. A sitemap shouldn't list URLs that have already moved, so this catches a second problem. Strip comments. Templates often keep old blocks commented out. Without removing comments, a naive count flags those too. Then open the CSV, filter to h1_count not equal to 1, and sort by h1_classes . Group the problems before you edit anything. If they cluster on one or two class pairs, fix the template and run the script again. What to do with the results The usual fix, when a CMS already prints the title as an H1 and a custom hero block adds another, is to change the hero heading to a paragraph or an H2 with the same CSS class. The page looks the same. The title in the CMS stays the only H1. If you have a pre-publish check, make sure it runs on every template, with no section-level exceptions that quietly skip the pages you ship most often. If your site is built from templates, I'd run this after every template change, not just once. It takes a few minutes, and the fix, once you can see the pattern, is usually one or two templates rather than a long page list. I'm Evgenii, founder of NeuroHelper AI, founded in 2024. I write about technical SEO for sites that change fast.

title: Zoom's Profile Picture Help Names a File Cap, Not a Pixel Size
author: Jacob Yang
summary: Zoom's help article for the web-portal profile picture, loaded on 27 November 2026, tells you the file types and a size cap. It does not tell you how many pixels to export. The page is titled Managing your profile picture on the Zoom web portal . Its schema.org dateModified is 2026-10-30 10:53:57. The only requirement I can quote is this: "Supported file types include JPG/JPEG, GIF, or PNG files smaller than 2MB." The add and change steps repeat that sentence, and they mention an optional crop area. They do not mention a width, a minimum edge, a recommended square, or a circular display. There is a second official number, and it does not agree. Release notes for Web , fetched the same day, have a schema.org dateModified of 2026-11-23 11:55:32. Under the heading "October 19, 2026," a general feature titled "Profile picture size limit increase" says users can upload profile photos "up to 10MB instead of the previous 2MB limit." That entry even links back to the help article. The help article, whose dateModified is eleven days later, still prints "smaller than 2MB." I am not going to pick a winner. I measured file sizes against both caps, and I did not invent a pixel size that neither page stated. I pointed the product link at ProfessionalHeadshot, an AI professional headshot generator, and the short page it keeps on zoom profile picture size . That generator typically returns forty to a hundred professional headshots from a small set of uploaded photos, usually in under an hour. I did not run it on the fixtures below. The landing page does recommend a square of at least 400×400 pixels, and 800×800 or higher for sharper display, and it describes the on-screen photo as a circle. Those are the product page's words, fetched today. They are not official Zoom specifications, and I did not measure live Zoom CSS. The measurement I can actually run is local: export a square, apply an inscribed circular mask, and see how much of the square is lost, which features get clipped, and whether common export sizes still read after that crop. Nothing here was uploaded to Zoom, and nothing was sent through the product. A local inscribed circle, not a client claim The geometry does not depend on Zoom. For a W×W square, an inscribed circle of diameter W keeps π/4 of the area, about 78.54 percent, and discards the four corners. The largest axis-aligned square that still fits inside that circle has side W/√2, about 0.7071 W, and occupies half of the original square. Content inside that inner square is fully visible. Content in the four corner wedges is gone. The four side lobes between the inner square and the circle stay in the picture, but they sit close to the edge. I built two 2048-pixel fixtures in Pillow 13.0.0. Neither fixture is a camera portrait of anyone. The first is a geometric badge: concentric rings at 0.50, 1/√2, 0.85, and 0.95 of the radius, mid-side ticks just inside the circle, a stroke around that inner safe square, and purple chevrons in the four corners. The second is a face-like stand-in made of ovals: a wide shoulder mass, a darker hair mass, a head oval slightly above mid-frame, and two small ellipses plus a short bar as features. I stored a label map for head, hair, shoulders, and features so clip fractions come from known pixels, not from a later guess. The circular mask used for counts is a hard threshold on distance from the pixel center: a pixel is inside if that distance is at most W/2. The figures use a slightly antialiased mask so the edge is not jaggy, but the numbers below always use the hard mask. Every resize uses LANCZOS, passed explicitly. Pillow's Image.resize documentation, fetched today, defaults to BICUBIC when the filter is omitted, and I did not want that default silently mixed in. The run was 27 November 2026, 13:43:36 to 13:43:41 Asia/Shanghai, on Python 3.13.5 with NumPy 2.5.5. Eighteen unit tests passed. The companion folder has the fixtures, the script, results.json , and the tests. How much of the square actually goes away At 2048×2048, the hard mask kept 3,294,288 of 4,194,304 pixels, or 78.5419 percent. That is 0.002 percentage points above π/4 (78.5398 percent). The 900,016 pixels outside the circle are 21.46 percent of the square. At the other export sizes I used, the measured fraction stayed between 78.53 and 78.69 percent; the coarsest grid, 128 pixels, was the farthest from the ideal, as you would expect. On the badge, the corner chevrons were a complete loss: all 10,862 of those pixels sat outside the circle. The mid-side ticks were a complete keep: all 2,624 pixels stayed in. Every ring, including the 0.95 ring, was fully inside at this resolution. The safe-square stroke was almost a complete keep, and the four pixels that leaked are the interesting part. The corners of that inner square lie on the circle. A stroke drawn on the square therefore puts a few pixels just outside the hard mask. Of 46,144 stroke pixels, four were clipped, a fraction of 0.0087 percent. If you treat the inner square as a "safe zone," keep the important content slightly inside it, not on the line. Figure 1. The same 2048-pixel badge, shown at 640 pixels. Left: the full square. Middle: pixels outside the inscribed circle, tinted. Right: the circular mask. The purple corner marks disappear. The mid-side ticks and the rings remain. This is a local mask, not a Zoom screenshot. A centered oval survives. A high crop starts to lose hair. The stand-in is deliberately plain. That is the point: I wanted known regions, not a studio portrait. With the figure centered the way I drew it, the circular mask clipped none of the head (1,048,100 pixels), none of the hair (695,918 pixels), and none of the features (50,184 pixels). The shoulders were a different story. Of 1,480,025 shoulder pixels, 449,569 sat outside the circle: 30.38 percent. The shoulder ellipse was drawn wide on purpose, so it would reach toward the lower corners. That is the part of a head-and-shoulders crop the circle takes first when the head itself is safely inside. I then shifted the whole figure up by 5, 10, and 15 percent of the frame, which is the usual "the head sits too high" mistake. Up-shift Hair clipped by the circle Head clipped by the circle Shoulders clipped by the circle 0% (centered) 0.00% 0.00% 30.38% 5% 3.26% 0.00% 26.15% 10% 8.81% 0.00% 21.29% 15% 14.56% 0.51% 14.98% The hair numbers are clip fractions of the hair pixels that remain on the square. At the 15 percent shift, part of the hair mass (and a sliver of the head oval) also left the top of the canvas before the circle was applied, so the region itself got smaller. Of the hair that was still in the square, 14.56 percent then fell outside the circle. The head was only nicked: 5,274 of 1,028,848 remaining head pixels, or 0.51 percent. The features, still near the center, were untouched at every shift I ran. The shoulder fraction moved the other way. As the figure rose, more of the shoulder ellipse entered the frame from the bottom, and a smaller share of it sat in the lower corners. A crop that is too high does not only cut hair. It also changes how much of the torso the circle still shows. Figure 2. Centered stand-in, then the same figure after a 15 percent upward shift, each as a square and as a circle. The features stay in. The hair starts to go. This is a labeled drawing, not a photograph, and not a Zoom upload. A wide source loses the sides before the circle does any work If the source is not already square, a center crop to 1:1 happens first. I placed the same 2048-pixel stand-in onto a wider canvas, then took the centered square, then applied the circle. A 16:9 canvas at height 2048 is 3641×2048 after int(round(2048 * 16 / 9)) . The side strips removed by the square crop are 1,593 pixels of width, or 1,593/3,641 of the canvas, 43.75 percent. A 4:3 canvas at the same height is 2731×2048; the square crop discards 683/2,731 of it, 25.01 percent. Those fractions are a little above the exact 7/16 and 1/4 because the rounded widths are 3641 and 2731, not 3640.889 and 2730.667. After that square crop, the remaining frame was the same centered stand-in I started with, so the circle's effect did not change: head and hair still unclipped, shoulders still 30.38 percent gone. The wide-source loss is in the side strips, not in an extra bite from the circle. If you start from a 16:9 still and let a center square crop do the work, you have already thrown away more than two fifths of the file before the circular mask is applied. That is a reason to square the frame yourself, with the subject where you want it, rather than hoping a later crop will guess. Common export sizes, and the official file cap I exported both fixtures at 128, 256, 400, 800, 1024, 1080, and 2048 pixels. Each size was written as a PNG, and also as a JPEG at qualities 85 and 70 with 4:2:0 chroma (Pillow subsampling=2 ). The 400 and 800 sizes are in the list because the product page names them, not because Zoom published them. 128 and 256 are undersized on purpose. 1024, 1080, and 2048 are larger squares people actually export. Every file I wrote sat comfortably under both official caps, under either a 10^6 or a 2^20 reading of "MB." The largest was the 2048-pixel badge JPEG at quality 85: 257,730 bytes, about 13 percent of 2,000,000 and about 12 percent of 2 MiB. The smallest was the 128-pixel stand-in JPEG at quality 70: 2,119 bytes. On these drawings, the 2MB figure printed on the help page was not the binding constraint. I did not encode a camera photograph, and I am not claiming a noisy 2048-pixel PNG from a real camera would land in the same place. PNG byte size also did not grow monotonically with the edge length. The 2048-pixel badge PNG, which is the original drawing with large flat fills, weighed 51,411 bytes. After a LANCZOS resize, the 800-pixel PNG occupied 167,802 bytes, and the 1080-pixel PNG occupied 230,373 bytes. Downsampling introduced more unique edge colors than the source had, and those mid-size files compressed worse. I would not use PNG length as a proxy for "how much image is there." What survives when the circle is later shown small I still do not have an official display diameter, so I will not pretend 96 or 400 pixels is "the Zoom tile." I did run a local what-if: take each export, resize it with LANCZOS to 96, 160, 240, or 400 pixels, and measure the peak-to-peak luminance in a thin band around the 0.95-radius ring, against a native export at that same display size. That metric is coarse. A soft ring can still have a wide min-to-max if some dark and light pixels remain, so I am not treating the ratio as a quality score. The useful reading is narrower. At a 400-pixel display, the 128-pixel export, which has to be upsampled, kept a 0.95-ring contrast of 200 against a native 400-pixel contrast of 242, a ratio of 0.826. Exports of 400 and 2048 both measured 242. The 800-pixel export measured 241. Once the export was at least the display size, this particular ring was essentially intact. The 128-pixel file was the one that had to be enlarged, and it was the one that lagged. The visual comparison is clearer than the contrast ratio. I took the circled badge at 128, 256, 400, and 800 pixels and zoomed each one to 400 pixels with nearest-neighbor resampling, so any softness is in the export, not in a later smooth resize. Figure 3. The same circular badge, exported at 128, 256, 400, and 800 pixels, then enlarged to 400 pixels with nearest-neighbor zoom so any softness is in the file. The 128-pixel export is the one that turns the rings into stairs. I did not capture a meeting tile. On this worksheet, 128 and 256 are the sizes I would skip. I would export a square bigger than any tile I actually expect to see, keep the important content inside that inner safe square, and treat the official file cap as a ceiling I did not come close to on these fixtures. I would use 400 or 800 only as sizes a product page named, not as a Zoom specification I had found. And I would look at the corners before I exported, because the circle will take them whether or not anyone printed a pixel size. Limits Everything above comes from two synthetic fixtures on disk. I did not open the Zoom client, I did not upload a file, and I did not measure the live app or the web portal. The help article I loaded on 27 November 2026 has no pixel size and no display shape. I left those blanks empty rather than filling them in. The inscribed circle is a model I chose because that is how the avatar is commonly described, including on the product page I used as a landing; I did not measure Zoom CSS today. The 2MB cap is the figure still printed on the help article. The 10MB cap is the figure in the 19 October 2026 web-portal release notes. I reported file sizes against both and did not reconcile the two pages. Peak-to-peak ring contrast is a coarse check, not a substitute for looking at the zoomed ladder. PNG lengths on these flat drawings are not a guide to photographic PNG lengths. I did not test GIF, and I did not test a file over either cap. The fixtures, the script, and today's results.json live in devto-ph-zoom-profile-picture-size-code/ . python3 measure_zoom_crop.py rebuilds the tables and the three figures; python3 test_measure_zoom_crop.py is the check I ran after the measurement.

title: Avoiding Partially Written Export Files in GBase 8a with Python UDFs
author: Michael
summary: GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP database from GBASE, can export over ftp and sftp . When the export is large — tens of GB — the target file takes time to finish writing. If a downstream job picks it up mid-export, it reads an incomplete file , which shows up as inconsistent data or parse errors. This post uses Python UDFs to add ftp / sftp rename support so the file only becomes visible when it is complete. The idea Downstream consumers usually scan for files matching a rule, for example *.csv under a load directory. Making an unfinished file fail that rule can be done two ways, and they can be combined: Name does not match — target is .csv , temporary file is .csv.tmp Path does not match — write to a temporary directory first Two steps Export to a temporary file (different suffix, or a temporary directory). Once the export finishes, use the protocol's rename to switch the temporary name to the final one — changing the suffix or moving across directories. FTP rename UDF Stored under gclusterdb , taking host, username, password, source name, target name . Port customisation is not implemented; extend it if you are not on the default ftp port: use gclusterdb ; drop function if exists ftpRename ; create function ftpRename ( server varchar ( 100 ) , username varchar ( 100 ) , password varchar ( 100 ) , sourceFilename varchar ( 1000 ) , targetFilename varchar ( 1000 ) ) returns varchar $$ from ftplib import FTP ftp = FTP ( server ) ftp . login ( username , password ) ftp . rename ( sourceFilename , targetFilename ) ftp . close ( ) return 'OK' $$ language plpythonu ; Calling it: gbase > select ftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv' ) ; +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | ftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv' ) | +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | OK | +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ 1 row in set ( Elapsed : 00 : 00 : 00.08 ) SFTP rename UDF The standard Python library does not speak sftp, so this example uses pysftp ( pip install pysftp ). Everything else matches the FTP version: use gclusterdb ; drop function if exists sftpRename ; create function sftpRename ( server varchar ( 100 ) , v_username varchar ( 100 ) , v_password varchar ( 100 ) , sourceFilename varchar ( 1000 ) , targetFilename varchar ( 1000 ) ) returns varchar $$ import pysftp with pysftp . Connection ( server , username = v_username , password = v_password ) as sftp : sftp . rename ( sourceFilename , targetFilename ) sftp . close ( ) return 'OK' $$ language plpythonu ; gbase > select sftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv' ) ; +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | sftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv' ) | +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | OK | +------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ 1 row in set ( Elapsed : 00 : 00 : 00.08 ) The full flow gbase > select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',' ; Query OK , 3 rows affected ( Elapsed : 00 : 00 : 00.32 ) gbase > select gclusterdb . sftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv' ) ; +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | gclusterdb . sftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv' ) | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | OK | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ 1 row in set ( Elapsed : 00 : 00 : 00.43 ) The temporary file can live in a different directory , provided the account has write permission there. This example uses both a temporary tmp directory and a .tmp suffix: gbase > select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',' ; Query OK , 3 rows affected ( Elapsed : 00 : 00 : 00.44 ) gbase > select gclusterdb . sftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/t1_2.csv' ) ; +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | gclusterdb . sftprename ( '10.0.2.201' , 'gbase' , 'gbase1234' , '/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' , '/home/gbase/t1_2.csv' ) | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | OK | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ 1 row in set ( Elapsed : 00 : 00 : 00.44 ) Both the export and the rename run inside the gbase client, and the consumer's scan rule never matches a .tmp file. Handing atomic visibility to rename means even a tens-of-GB export no longer needs a sleep timer or a human "is it done yet" check — a small UDF turns the database's own export into a safe handoff.

title: Add a Product to the Shopify Cart from a Chatbot (With Variant Checks and Error Handling)
author: Aylelite
summary: Add a Product to the Shopify Cart from a Chatbot (With Variant Checks and Error Handling) The risky part of "add to cart" in a chatbot is adding the wrong variant, or failing silently when an item is sold out. Here's a small, safe version using Shopify's Ajax Cart API. Load the product and its variants Every product page has a JSON endpoint at /products/.js. javascript async function getProduct(handle) { const res = await fetch( /products/${handle}.js ); if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Product not found'); return res.json(); } Find the variant the shopper chose Match on the options, not on a guess. javascript function findVariant(product, wanted) { // wanted example: { Size: 'M', Color: 'Green' } const names = product.options.map(o => (typeof o === 'string' ? o : o.name)); return product.variants.find(v => names.every((name, i) => !wanted[name] || v[ option${i + 1} ] === wanted[name]) ); } If no variant matches, ask the shopper again instead of adding anything. Add to cart and handle errors javascript async function addToCart(variantId, quantity = 1) { const res = await fetch('/cart/add.js', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ items: [{ id: variantId, quantity }] }), }); if (res.ok) return { ok: true }; const err = await res.json().catch(() => ({})); return { ok: false, message: err.description || err.message || 'Could not add this item.' }; } Shopify returns an error with a readable message when an item is sold out or the quantity isn't available, so show it to the shopper. Put it together javascript async function handleAdd(handle, wanted, qty) { const product = await getProduct(handle); const variant = findVariant(product, wanted); if (!variant) return 'Which size and color would you like?'; if (!variant.available) return 'Sorry, that option is sold out. Want to see similar items?'; const result = await addToCart(variant.id, qty); return result.ok ? Added ${product.title} (${variant.title}). View cart or keep browsing? : result.message; } Tips Confirm size and color in chat before calling the API. Always show "View cart" and "Keep browsing" afterwards. Test quantity above one, sold-out variants, and a phone browser. If your theme uses a cart drawer, refresh it after adding. Wrap-up Add to cart in a chatbot is just three checks: the right product, the right variant, and a clear message when something fails. Get those right and the rest is design.

title: Introducing Bord: a Rails engine for your dashboard
author: Rails Designer
summary: Time for something new again! It is called Bord (Dutch for—you guessed it right—board, though it also could mean “plate”). It is in short a Rails engine for a dashboard with metrics, lists, categories and pages . Every widget runs your own code: ActiveRecord queries, Stripe calls, Good Job stats, Action Mailbox records. This gem’s code has lived (in a less configurable) setup in my apps for some time and is the screen I check for new signups and run quick actions (log in as user, re-run webhook using Fuik ). What it can do A metric shows one value, such as MRR, signups today, failed jobs or the Stripe balance. Add href and the value becomes a link. A list shows recent records, such as new users, recent charges or failed jobs. Each item can link to a record and have its own actions. A category groups widgets and sets their order on the page. A page lists records and can show one record in detail. I use one for customers and one for charges. An action calls a method on a record: refund a charge, retry a job, log in as a user. You add it to a widget or to an item in a list, and Bord renders a button. I use Bord to see the most important stats for my app. How to configure bundle add bord bin/rails generate bord:install The installer creates config/bord/dashboard.rb and mounts the engine at /bord . Bord loads every file under config/bord/**/*.rb , so you can split widgets across files. # config/bord/dashboard.rb Bord . draw do title "Spinal Labs" category :financials , label : "Financials" , position : 1 do metric :mrr , label : "MRR" , value : -> { Current . account . mrr . format } list :recent_users , label : "Recent users" , items : -> { User . order ( created_at : :desc ) . limit ( 5 ) } end end Add categories, metrics and lists to that file. Pages use Bord.page . Set the parent controller in an initializer: # config/initializers/bord.rb Bord . configure do | config | config . parent_controller = "Admin::BaseController" config . brand_hue = 250 end In production, /bord returns 404 until parent_controller is set. That controller is the only authorization gate. Anyone with access to it can use the dashboard. Development and test work without configuration. bin/rails generate bord:presets lists presets for Solid Queue, Good Job, Sidekiq, Stripe, Active Storage, Action Mailbox and plain users. Pick the ones you want, and the generator appends their code to config/bord/presets.rb . A preset is a JSON file, so other gems can ship one. How it works [AD] Spinal CMS: Git-based CMS for static site generators Bord is a small engine. Most of it is just Ruby objects and ERB templates. value and items are lambdas. Bord runs them per request with instance_exec in the controller’s view context, so Current , route helpers and bord.page_path work inside. If you want a number, you write a query. The page loads empty. Each widget renders its label and an empty value or list. On mount, Attractive.js requests /bord/data . The server responds with a list of actions: { action : "replace" , target : "widget-mrr-value" , template : "bord-value" , data : { value : "$28,400" } } The Attract addon renders a cached <template> for each action and applies it. A widget can replace a value, append an entry or set a link. . An action names a record by GlobalID and a method: { label : "Refund" , confirm : "Refund this charge?" , variant : :danger , action : { record : charge . to_gid . to_s , method : :refund , customer_id : charge . id } } On submit, Bord finds the record, calls the method with the other parameters, and refreshes the widget. Bord checks the submitted action against the actions you declared. Lists accept model instances. If a model defines to_bord , Bord uses it for the title, description and link. Future ideas Things I think of adding are: an API layer (widgets are queries and actions are records plus methods, so exposing them as JSON is simple). Actions could need more input. Today an action is a method plus flat parameters. I want forms: add a note to a refund, pick a reason, enter an amount. Then a refund action can take a note and a reason as well as the charge id. I also want charts next to metrics and authorization per action instead of one controller gate. This is, as I often do, a pre-v1/initial release to see what you think of this idea. Have a play with it and see if the DSL/API for adding widgets makes sense. I just released 0.5.0 of Bord. Give it a try and then a star . ✨😊

title: Lorem Ipsum Isn't Lazy — It's How Good Layouts Get Built
author: binothehen-code10
summary: Lorem Ipsum Isn't Lazy — It's How Good Layouts Get Built Every designer has done it: you open a blank page, type a headline, and then freeze, because the words aren't written yet. So you paste in some lorem ipsum, the layout suddenly makes sense, and you can finally see what you're building. That is exactly what placeholder text is for. It is not a shortcut or a sign of laziness. It is a tool that lets you judge a design on its own merits — typography, spacing, hierarchy, rhythm — before a single real sentence exists. Why meaningless text makes better designs Real copy is distracting. The moment a reviewer can read the words, they start editing the words. "Should this say 'customers' instead of 'clients'?" — and suddenly nobody is looking at the layout anymore. Lorem ipsum solves this because it means nothing. The eye treats it as texture, not language, so attention stays where it belongs: on how the page holds together. Printers have used it since the 1500s for exactly this reason, and web designers inherited the habit because it still works. How to use placeholder text properly A block of dummy text is only useful if you use it the way a real page will be used. Here is the workflow I follow: 1. Match the amount to the real content. If the final article will be 800 words, don't test the template with two short paragraphs. Generate the same volume the real page will carry, so you see the true shape of the layout — where it gets long, where it breathes, where it breaks. 2. Test the extremes. Generate a very short version (a few words) and a very long one (many paragraphs) and drop both into the same template. Headlines wrap, cards stretch, buttons move. A layout that survives both extremes will survive real content. 3. Check every breakpoint. Placeholder text behaves differently at mobile width than on desktop. Paste the same block in, resize the browser, and watch for awkward orphans, cramped line lengths, and columns that collapse badly. 4. Vary the lengths. Real pages mix short intros, long bodies, and tiny captions. If every test block is the same size, you are testing one layout, not the design system. A free generator that does the job in seconds You don't need a plugin or a paid tool for this. FakeXLab's Lorem Ipsum Generator is free, needs no sign-up, and runs entirely in your browser. You choose paragraphs, sentences, or words, set the amount, click Generate, and copy the text straight into your mockup. Because it generates by word and sentence count as well as paragraphs, you can build exactly the shape you need — a one-line button label, a three-sentence card description, or a full article's worth of body text for a long-form template. Build a complete mockup, not just a text block Placeholder text works best as part of a full fake page. Once the body copy is in place, fill the rest of the design with equally fictional data so the whole mockup feels real without exposing anyone's real information: Add a byline with the Random Name Generator so author cards and profile blocks look finished. Fill out sample forms and checkout screens with the Fake Address Generator — a complete fictional profile, address included, in one click. Protect any test accounts you create along the way with a strong password from the Password Generator . Everything on FakeXLab is fictional and for testing only, and nothing you generate is stored or sent anywhere — it all happens in your browser. The mistakes to avoid Placeholder text is a design tool, not content. Three mistakes turn it into a problem: Shipping it live. Lorem ipsum on a published page looks unfinished and hurts trust. Replace every block with real copy before launch — run a quick search for "lorem" across the site as a final check. Testing with one perfect block. If your test text is always the same length, your layout only works at that length. Real content is messy; test messy. Using real copy too early. Drafting final words before the layout is settled means rewriting both when the design changes. Get the shape right first, then write into it. The takeaway Good layouts are built before the words arrive. Lorem ipsum lets you see the design clearly, test it honestly, and hand it over with confidence — and a free generator like FakeXLab's makes the whole thing take seconds instead of an afternoon of copy-pasting. Next time you start a mockup, generate the text first, build around it, and let the design speak before the content does.

title: Agentic CRMs That Scale With Enterprise Growth
author: Sam Amderson
summary: An agentic CRM enterprise setup scales when agents write to customer records through guarded, repeatable paths instead of direct, unlimited updates. Most teams hit the same wall. A pilot with three agents works well, then thirty agents start overwriting each other's changes. Duplicate records appear, owners lose trust, and sales leaders stop reading the data. The fix is not a smarter model. It is a write layer that handles conflicts, retries, and approvals before volume grows. This article covers what breaks first, how to write agent updates safely, and which actions need a human sign-off. What Makes an Agentic CRM Enterprise Architecture Different? A chatbot reads a record and drafts a reply. An agent reads, decides, and writes back. That one change turns your CRM from a database people edit into a system that software edits at machine speed. Teams planning an agentic crm enterprise rollout therefore design for concurrency first and features second. Agents Change Who Writes to the Record Humans edit one record at a time, and they edit slowly. Agents update many records in parallel, from different triggers: an inbound email, a stage change, a scoring job. Each trigger may touch the same account within seconds. Without rules, the last writer wins and earlier updates vanish silently. Agentic CRM architecture must therefore treat every agent as a concurrent writer with an identity, a rate budget, and a fixed list of fields it may change. Ownership per field, not per record, keeps those rules simple enough to audit. Growth Multiplies Triggers, Not Just Records Enterprise growth adds more than rows. It adds regions, business units, integrations, and agents, and each addition creates new triggers. Ten agents with five triggers each produce fifty write paths. Tests for CRM agent scalability should count write paths, not records. An agentic CRM enterprise team that tracks only record volume sees a calm dashboard until two paths collide on one account. Counting paths early shows where to add queues, locks, or approvals before customers see wrong data. Quick check: Is an agentic CRM just a CRM with a chatbot? No. A chatbot answers questions from records. An agent changes records, so it needs write controls, an identity, and an audit trail that chat features never required. Where Does an Agentic CRM Break First as Volume Grows? An agentic CRM enterprise rollout fails in a predictable order. The table maps each growth stage to its first failure and the control that prevents it. This working model comes from common concurrency patterns, not from a benchmark. Growth stage What breaks first Guardrail Few agents, one trigger each Duplicate updates after retries Idempotency key on every write Many agents, shared accounts CRM write conflicts: the last writer wins Optimistic locking with a version check Many regions and business units Update bursts exceed what the CRM accepts Per-agent rate budget and a write queue Autonomous outbound actions Wrong action from weak context Agent autonomy gates with human approval CRM Write Conflicts Appear Before Volume Does Conflicts need only two agents and one account. Agent A reads a record at version four. Agent B reads the same version, writes its change, and moves the record to version five. Agent A then writes from stale data and erases B's change without any error. Logs show two successful updates, so nobody investigates. Optimistic locking prevents this. It rejects A's write because the version has moved, which forces a fresh read and a clean merge. Weak Context Turns Fast Agents Into Fast Mistakes In an agentic CRM enterprise stack, speed amplifies bad inputs. An agent that moves an opportunity stage based on a vague email thread can push a deal backward in seconds, and the forecast turns false. Require every write to carry its source, such as the email ID or call record, so reviewers can trace it. Then set a confidence floor. Below it, the agent proposes a change instead of applying it. Reviewers approve proposals in bulk, and trust grows with evidence. Quick check: Why not simply lock the whole record while an agent works? Locks stall every other agent and human on that account. A version check lets all writers proceed and rejects only the stale one, which keeps throughput high. How Do You Write Agent Updates to a CRM Safely? Three rules cover most failures. Use an idempotency key so retries never apply twice. Check the record version so stale writes fail loudly. Throttle each agent with a token bucket. The Python below implements all three against an in-memory stand-in for a CRM. Swap the InMemoryCrm calls for your CRM's SDK, and the pattern holds for any agentic CRM enterprise deployment. Run the file as it is to watch five concurrent agents update one record without losing a change. import threading import time class VersionConflict ( Exception ) : """Raised when a record changed after the agent read it.""" class InMemoryCrm : """Stand-in for a CRM API. Replace with your CRM's client.""" def __init__ ( self ) : self . _records = { } self . _lock = threading . Lock ( ) def create ( self , record_id , fields ) : with self . _lock : self . _records [ record_id ] = { "version" : 1 , "fields" : dict ( fields ) } def get ( self , record_id ) : with self . _lock : rec = self . _records [ record_id ] return rec [ "version" ] , dict ( rec [ "fields" ] ) def update ( self , record_id , fields , expected_version ) : with self . _lock : rec = self . _records [ record_id ] if rec [ "version" ] != expected_version : raise VersionConflict ( record_id ) rec [ "fields" ] . update ( fields ) rec [ "version" ] += 1 return rec [ "version" ] class TokenBucket : """Per-agent rate budget: `rate` writes per second, bursts up to `burst`.""" def __init__ ( self , rate , burst ) : self . rate = rate self . capacity = burst self . tokens = float ( burst ) self . updated = time . monotonic ( ) self . _lock = threading . Lock ( ) def take ( self ) : while True : with self . _lock : now = time . monotonic ( ) self . tokens = min ( self . capacity , self . tokens + ( now - self . updated ) * self . rate , ) self . updated = now if self . tokens >= 1 : self . tokens -= 1 return wait = ( 1 - self . tokens ) / self . rate time . sleep ( wait ) class SafeWriter : """Idempotent, version-checked, rate-limited writes for one agent.""" def __init__ ( self , crm , rate = 20 , burst = 5 , max_retries = 5 ) : self . crm = crm self . bucket = TokenBucket ( rate , burst ) self . max_retries = max_retries self . _seen = { } self . _lock = threading . Lock ( ) def write ( self , record_id , fields , idempotency_key , source ) : with self . _lock : if idempotency_key in self . _seen : return self . _seen [ idempotency_key ] # retry: do nothing twice for attempt in range ( self . max_retries ) : self . bucket . take ( ) version , current = self . crm . get ( record_id ) changes = { k : v for k , v in fields . items ( ) if current . get ( k ) != v } if not changes : result = version # nothing to change, no extra write else : changes [ "last_update_source" ] = source # every write is traceable try : result = self . crm . update ( record_id , changes , version ) except VersionConflict : time . sleep ( 0.01 * ( 2 ** attempt ) ) # back off, re-read, retry continue with self . _lock : self . _seen [ idempotency_key ] = result return result raise RuntimeError ( f "Gave up on {record_id} after {self.max_retries} conflicts" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : crm = InMemoryCrm ( ) crm . create ( "acct-1" , { "stage" : "prospect" } ) writer = SafeWriter ( crm , rate = 200 , burst = 20 ) jobs = [ ( "a1" , { "stage" : "qualified" } , "email-101" ) , ( "a2" , { "owner" : "emea-team" } , "routing-7" ) , ( "a3" , { "score" : 82 } , "scoring-job-3" ) , ( "a4" , { "region" : "EMEA" } , "enrichment-9" ) , ( "a5" , { "next_step" : "demo" } , "call-55" ) , ( "a1" , { "stage" : "qualified" } , "email-101" ) , # duplicate retry ] threads = [ threading . Thread ( target = writer . write , args = ( "acct-1" , f , k , s ) ) for k , f , s in jobs ] for t in threads : t . start ( ) for t in threads : t . join ( ) version , fields = crm . get ( "acct-1" ) print ( "version:" , version ) print ( "fields:" , fields ) assert fields [ "stage" ] == "qualified" assert fields [ "owner" ] == "emea-team" assert fields [ "score" ] == 82 assert fields [ "region" ] == "EMEA" assert fields [ "next_step" ] == "demo" Quick check: What does the idempotency key actually protect against? Retries. If a network call times out and the agent sends the same update again, the key makes the second attempt a no-op instead of a second change. When Can an Agent Act on a Customer Record Without Approval? Agent autonomy gates answer that question for any agentic CRM enterprise team. Tie each gate to business impact, not to model confidence alone. The table below shows one starting set for enterprise CRM automation with AI agents. Impact level Example action Rule Low Add a call note or a tag The agent applies it and logs the source Medium Change a stage or an owner The agent applies it above the confidence floor, otherwise it proposes High Send outbound messages, edit contract fields, delete records A human approves first Review the gates every quarter. When reviewers approve an agent's proposals for a sustained period without edits, move that action one level down. Keep the approval log as well. It becomes your evidence when auditors ask who changed a record, and why. Quick check: Who should own the confidence floor? The team that owns the business outcome, not the team that built the agent. Revenue operations usually owns the floor, and engineering enforces it in code. A Two-Week Plan to Harden Your CRM Write Path For an agentic CRM enterprise team, start with visibility, then add controls one at a time. In week one, list every agent and every trigger that writes to your CRM, and count the write paths. Add an idempotency key to each path, and log every version conflict you see. Those logs show where agents collide most. In week two, add the version check and a rate budget for each agent. Set a confidence floor for stage and owner changes, and choose one high-impact action to place behind human approval. At the end, review the conflict log with the team that owns the data. If one account or field attracts most collisions, split ownership of that field before you add more agents. Repeat the cycle each time you add an agent, because every new agent creates new write paths that need the same checks.

title: I Tested the Viral AI 3D Web Games on X: Here Is the Stack, GPU Reality, and What Prompts Still Can't Do
author: boluo
summary: Let's be honest: most "AI-generated game" clips on X look amazing for five seconds and fall apart the moment you actually try to play them. When a new wave of 3D browser games started racking up millions of views—right after GPT-6 Astra blew up 3D asset showcases and Claude Opus 5.5 started churning out procedural animations—I wanted to know what was actually running under the hood. On November 27, 2026, I dug through the 11 biggest viral builds from this wave, cloned the open-source repos ( turbo-kart-rally and voxel-musou ) onto an older laptop with an integrated Intel UHD 620 GPU, and tested the model APIs they used: ✅ Where this stack shines: Shipping a playable 3D browser prototype in 2 to 7 days with Three.js ⚠️ Where prompts alone fail: Branching RPG narratives, multiplayer state sync, and low-end GPU optimization Here are the 5 biggest engineering lessons I found after tearing these 11 projects apart. 🏎️ 1. "Zero External Assets" Does Not Mean "Zero GPU Load" One of the coolest open-source repos in this batch is an MIT-licensed Mario Kart clone ( turbo-kart-rally ) written in pure Three.js without a single build tool. The README states 100% procedural assets —downloading zero .gltf models and zero texture files: 🏁 8 procedural racers: Built out of Three.js geometric primitives and color palettes, each with custom speed, acceleration, handling, and weight stats 🏎️ Complete 100cc race loop: Connects the title screen, character select, 3-lap tracking ( LAP 1/3 ), item boxes, and Shift drift boosts Another developer pushed this procedural trick even further, packing an Underwater Shipwreck Exploration game (diving into a wreck to locate the ancient Antikythera mechanism) into a single 3MB HTML file —synthesizing deep-sea lighting, geometry, and underwater sound on the fly. People see "3MB file" or "no external models" and assume it runs on a potato. I benchmarked the kart racer on an Intel UHD 620 integrated GPU to test that theory: 🖥️ Browser hardware acceleration ON ( 800×450 ): Ran at ~39 FPS —completely playable, just slightly tight on sharp turns 🐢 Software rendering / GPU OFF ( 480×270 ): Collapsed to 1.5–6.5 FPS , making steering impossible Procedural code skips asset downloads and bundlers, not WebGL draw calls. To survive on low-end laptops, you still have to manually cut dynamic shadows, vehicle counts, and canvas resolution. 🎯 2. Every Working AI Game Secretly Uses the Same 5 Math Mechanics Why can an LLM one-shot a playable kart racer or turf shooter, yet choke on a narrative detective game? Look at the other browser builds in this batch: 🔫 #1 Viral Sci-Fi Squad Shooter: Wear heavy armor, push down urban streets with AI teammates, shoot enemy soldiers, and capture control points. Built with Claude Opus 5.5 and Three.js by a creator who never read a line of code—proving gunfire pacing, squad cover behavior, and capture feedback are human design calls. 🎨 Splatoon-Style Ink Painter (Claude Opus 5.5): Spray ink on the floor to claim territory in your team's color and dive into friendly ink to swim faster. 🌊 Voxel Water & Shader Test (Claude Opus 5.5): Classic blocky mountains and trees, upgraded with planar water reflections, sunbeams cutting through leaves, and day-to-night transitions. 🚀 Sky Reach Planetary Landing: Fly a spaceship toward a distant planet, punch through the atmosphere, land on the surface, and step out on foot. Strip away the paint and all 11 games rely on just five math-friendly mechanics : 🏃 Free movement + camera follow 🛤️ Path or waypoint progression 🟦 Grid-cell surface color changes 💥 Crowd collision & hitboxes 🔢 Procedural environment math None of them require branching dialogue trees, long-term economy balancing, or multiplayer netcode. LLMs shine when the core loop reduces to vectors, state machines, and distance checks. 🛠️ 3. Three.js, Tripo, Blender, and Unity Are Sequential—And You Can't Skip Blender Beginners constantly ask: "Should I use Three.js, Tripo, Blender, or Unity?" The creators who built character-heavy games chained them together across four distinct jobs: 🖼️ 2D Image Generation: Locks the character's visual look 🧊 Tripo: Converts that 2D image or text into a 3D mesh 🛠️ Blender: Fixes topology, rigging, and animations (the one step prompts cannot skip) 🎮 Unity or Three.js: Assembles the final game loop Here is how two viral builds used that pipeline: 🌹 The Little Prince 3D Planet (16 days, 3.46M views, ~10K bookmarks): Walk the Little Prince around his tiny planet to visit his rose and the king. Locking the 2D character art first before converting to 3D, cleaning up in Blender, and assembling in Unity made the book's cast recognizable immediately. 🕸️ Spider-Man City Swinging: Leap off rooftops, swing on webs above traffic and pedestrians, and run up building facades. After fixing the animations in Blender , the creator skipped Unity and exported straight back into a Three.js web page. ⚔️ 4. A Combat Room Takes 10 Minutes; A Game Loop Takes Human Choreography My favorite open-source repo in the list is Voxel Musou ( voxel-musou ), where you play as Zhao Yun slashing through crowds of voxel soldiers with combos, dodge rolls, and musou specials. The creator wrote that this was their childhood dream game. Version 1 was literally just Zhao Yun hitting soldiers in an empty space. What turned it into an actual game was the screen-by-screen flow they wired up afterward: 📜 Starting at the main menu and selecting Chapter 1 ( Hulao Gate · Normal ) 🛡️ Choosing Liu Bei, Guan Yu, or Zhang Fei on the Shu-Han route 🎙️ Watching a voiced cutscene with subtitles about Dong Zhuo and Yuan Shao's coalition 🎯 Entering the battlefield with a live 61m distance HUD ( Defeat Dong Zhuo's forces in front of Sishui Pass ) Even in the Call of Duty MW2 + Skate 3 + Minecraft mashup (7.5M views, ~30K likes—shoot MW2 guns, hit J to kickflip a skateboard, and shoot blocks in a Minecraft world), the magic is in the boundaries. Built in Rust on the open-source IW4L runtime, it keeps its repo clean by downloading ~125MB of vanilla Minecraft assets from Mojang's official servers on first launch, requiring a legal Steam copy of MW2, and disabling skateboarding if Xbox 360 Skate 3 's default.xex is missing. 🔌 5. How to Route claude-opus-5-5 Without Burning $2,400 Blindly One creator let an AI run on a gaming laptop for 36 hours straight to build an old-school RPG (character creation, towns, combat), spending $2,400 across API calls and generated art/music. Across the builds that disclosed their model stack, Claude Opus 5.5 was the main workhorse. When I test claude-opus-5-5 against other models on Three.js prototypes, I avoid juggling separate vendor keys and billing dashboards by routing requests through Crazyrouter and swapping only the model string: https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1 Three quick gotchas from my API verification on November 27, 2026: 🔗 SDK path suffix: Use the /v1 suffix above for OpenAI-compatible SDKs, or pass the root domain without /v1 for the native Anthropic SDK ( claude-opus-5-5 via /v1/messages returned HTTP 200 in 10.2 seconds ) 💰 Budget check: Check the daily-verified model pricing table before kicking off multi-hour agent loops 🔍 Query GET /v1/models directly: Even when claude-opus-5-5 's web detail page returned a 404 during my check, GET /v1/models confirmed the model ID was active and routable Every one of these 11 builds still needs save systems, gamepad input abstraction, low-end GPU profiling, and audio mixing before commercial release—but they all prove the same rule: build the movement and fun with ugly boxes first, and worry about the art last.

title: Budgeting a Launch’s Visual Assets: VisualGPT Black Friday Plans Compared
author: chloe_lai
summary: A small product launch can need more visual assets than expected: a landing-page hero, social cards, product images, and a short announcement video. The difficult part is often planning iterations. One exported asset may follow several candidate generations, and a change to the launch message can send the whole set back for revision. VisualGPT is running a Black Friday promotion ending November 30. Its featured offers include a $204 annual Pro plan and two discounted Lifetime Credits packs. This promotional guide uses the pricing displayed on November 27, 2026, to explain how those options fit a developer’s asset-production budget. It does not claim benchmark results or an API integration. Separate the release backlog from the generation budget Start with deliverables, not credits. A useful asset backlog names the placement, dimensions, source material, and acceptance criteria for each item. A homepage hero needs a different composition from a social preview; a product image needs accurate details even when the surrounding scene changes. For a hypothetical launch, list one hero, three social cards, and two product illustrations. Those six deliverables do not imply six generations. You might explore several compositions, reject outputs with incorrect details, and revise the selected version. Record those attempts separately so the budget reflects the work required to reach an acceptable asset. VisualGPT presents product photography, portrait editing, and video creation on its homepage. Check the chosen tool’s actual credit requirement before assigning a budget. Different models and settings can change consumption; video should have its own estimate rather than borrowing an image allowance. What the Black Friday offers include The featured annual Pro offer is $204 per year , with 2,000 credits per month . The page states a $36 saving against the regular annual price. Dividing the annual payment by twelve gives a $17 monthly equivalent, but this is an annual purchase, not a $17 monthly billing option. The featured one-time packs are 5,000 credits for $119 , compared with the displayed $149 price, and 10,000 credits for $199 , compared with $299. The respective savings are $30 and $100. These are different payment and allocation models. An annual subscription’s monthly credits should not be treated as a single immediately available annual balance. Lifetime Credits are a finite purchased balance that the pricing page says can be retained until used. “Lifetime” does not mean unlimited generation. Choose around release cadence An annual plan is worth comparing when visual production continues between releases: documentation illustrations, recurring announcements, product updates, and regular content. Evaluate whether the monthly allocation matches that recurring workload and check the validity rules before purchasing. A one-time pack is a different fit for uneven work. A team might prepare a launch this month, spend the next month on engineering, and return to campaign assets later. Credits that remain available until used can align with that pattern. The larger pack has a lower price per credit, but a higher upfront payment. Compare expected use before optimizing the unit price. A cheap unused balance is still money spent. Existing subscribers can also compare a pack for temporary extra demand: the official pricing FAQ says subscriptions and packs can be used together. Track the cost of accepted assets A simple spreadsheet or local text file is enough to improve estimates. Keep an asset ID, target placement, model and settings, credits consumed, revision reason, and acceptance status. This is a manual planning suggestion, not a claim that VisualGPT exposes these fields through an API. For a completed batch, divide the credits actually consumed by the number of accepted assets. This gives a practical measure for the next similar batch. Keep image and video records separate, and do not compare materially different settings as though they had the same cost. Review at the final placement size. Check product details, visible text, faces, hands, and cropping. If an image needs correction in a separate editor, include that work in the production estimate rather than attributing the entire result to generation. Check usage rights alongside the budget The homepage describes commercial-use rights for qualifying images generated with eligible paid subscriptions or Lifetime Credits, subject to terms and model and source-asset restrictions. That is not permission to upload arbitrary third-party images or reproduce protected branding. Keep a record of the source assets you are entitled to use. Review applicable conditions for the actual output and workflow, especially when producing client deliverables. A promotional price does not remove those requirements. Turn the offer into a concrete release decision Before the November 30 end date, identify the next batch of assets, check the required tools and generation settings, and compare recurring monthly demand with one-time demand. Confirm the price and conditions displayed at purchase. The annual Pro offer is the recurring-work option to evaluate; the featured credit packs are the flexible-balance options. You can explore the tools and current offer from the VisualGPT homepage . Prices are in USD and reflect the November 27, 2026 page display. This article was prepared with AI writing assistance; it reports official offer details rather than firsthand performance testing.

title: Vozelle: AI voice changer for mobile chat apps
author: Siqi
summary: What is Vozelle? Most voice changers force you to record audio, save the file, then manually upload it to chats. title: Designing an Omnichannel AI Chatbot for Smarter Customer Support
author: Lgo Chat
summary: Building an AI chatbot involves more than generating automated responses. Developers must consider how customer information, communication channels, business workflows, and human agents interact within a single system. An effective chatbot architecture should address five important components. 1. Centralized Conversation Management Customers frequently switch between websites, messaging applications, and email. Maintaining a unified conversation history helps prevent information loss and repetitive questions. A centralized messaging layer can normalize incoming messages from different channels before passing them to the chatbot. 2. Knowledge-Based Responses AI chatbot software can use approved knowledge sources, such as product documentation, frequently asked questions, and company policies, to provide more relevant responses. Developers should establish processes for updating these sources and handling questions that cannot be answered reliably. 3. Workflow Automation Connecting chatbots with business workflows enables conversations to trigger practical actions, such as: Creating customer support tickets Scheduling appointments Retrieving order information Categorizing customer inquiries Updating customer records Sensitive operations should include appropriate authentication and authorization checks. 4. Intelligent Human Handoff Not every customer inquiry should be handled automatically. Developers should establish escalation rules for unresolved questions, sensitive concerns, and requests for human assistance. Transferring the conversation history alongside the inquiry allows support agents to continue without asking customers to repeat themselves. 5. Performance Monitoring Evaluating chatbot performance requires more than measuring response speed. Development teams should also monitor resolution accuracy, escalation rates, customer satisfaction, and unsuccessful interactions. These metrics help identify weaknesses and guide continuous improvements. Conclusion A reliable omnichannel customer support system combines conversational AI, structured workflows, secure integrations, and human oversight. The objective of customer service automation should not be to eliminate human interaction entirely, but to ensure that each inquiry reaches the most appropriate resolution.
